prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case where a sharp, non-obvious theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) was followed years later by a decisive experiment (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) that created a whole field. It has been reproduced by many independent groups, extended to other moire systems, and has brought tunable correlated and topological matter within reach of a single device. That is a discovery with originality, clarity and lasting breadth. It also has the widest support in the opening round (top-three on five ballots, ranked on six), including my own second place, and its theory-plus-experiment structure fits the three-name limit better than most alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and timing. The experimental credit rests on the Jarillo-Herrero group, and first author Yuan Cao and other experimentalists (and parallel work such as the Dean and Young groups) are not carried in the supplied names. The nature of the superconducting state is still debated, and the discovery dates only to 2018, so a committee that weights long-term confirmation could reasonably call it early. Against my own first choice, B012, the case against is that I am too close to it: circuit QED is my own field and Chalmers colleagues are near it, and a second superconducting-circuit prize right after 2025 would need a clear distinction from macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. I therefore do not press it as the preferred outcome.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the optical lattice clock first as a clean, mature, instrument-driven advance, and treats the pulsar-timing gravitational-wave background as possibly premature.
responses.response: I agree that B015 is mature, unambiguous in its figure of merit and fairly credited to Katori and Ye, and I keep it as an alternative for that reason. I would qualify the idea that it must come first: it is a metrology achievement whose main payoffs (redefinition of the second, geodesy, dark-matter searches) are still prospective, while the moire discovery has already changed what condensed-matter physicists work on. I share his caution on pulsar timing; evidence at the 3-4 sigma level per array is not enough for me.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a natural theory-plus-experiment prize with a sharp prediction, broad impact and a mature, reproduced experiment.
responses.response: I agree with the structure he describes and with the three names, since Bistritzer and MacDonald made one joint prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experiment. I am less relaxed than he is about calling the discovery fully mature. The mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, so I would write the citation around the prediction and the observation of the phases and make no claim about their origin.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the clock first but also puts twisted bilayer graphene second, noting that recognition may be somewhat early because the discovery dates from 2018 and the superconducting mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously, and it is the main weakness of B017. But the discovery itself is robust: correlated insulators and superconducting domes are seen in many labs and devices, and the open question is interpretation, not existence. I would not let that count against a discovery prize, and I do not think waiting would improve the attribution. I do agree with her that Yuan Cao's omission from the credited names is a real injustice that the citation cannot repair.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators first, as an overdue conceptual change in band theory, and would give twisted bilayer graphene only two names, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual case for B051, but the allocation between the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D materials is contested, and the three-name cap forces out Mele or Hasan. On B017 I would keep Bistritzer, because the 2011 prediction was a joint paper and omitting him would give MacDonald credit that belongs to the pair.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first and sees it as a two-person prize with a clear division between Katori's concept and Ye's performance.
responses.response: I agree the credit split is clean. My reservation is only about relative weight: the clock refines a quantity we already measure very well, whereas moire systems opened an entirely new set of phenomena. I would not oppose B015 and have placed it among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the 2018 experiments as sufficiently mature given the unresolved superconducting mechanism.
How to treat the omission of Yuan Cao and other experimental contributors who are outside the credited names.
Whether a circuit QED prize (B012) is distinct enough from the 2025 macroscopic quantum tunnelling prize, and how to allocate the theory share between Girvin and Blais.
Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize pairing a quantum-technology achievement with a materials one, which the three-person cap makes hard.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue for B012: I work on circuit QED theory, I am a Chalmers colleague of Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, and I direct WACQT, so I discount my own first-ranked choice and do not make it my preferred configuration. For B017, B015 and the other shortlisted candidates, no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
